154.open: Whether antennae cut within the scape in late mantid nymphs regenerate as legs, and whether these carry raptorial foreleg identity; the claim rests on one clear and one partial case among six regenerates and was never repeated.
154.test: Cut antennae within the scape in late-instar Sphodromantis or Hierodula nymphs reared at 17–20 °C; score regenerates for femoral spines and tibial teeth, and compare Sex combs reduced, Antennapedia, homothorax and Distal-less expression with fore- and midlegs.

155.verdict: Leg segments on beetle antennae read as regenerates; consistent, never re-tested
155.why: Przibram read tarsus-like segments on three wild-caught beetles' antennae as heteromorphic regenerates and rejected ganglionic control of appendage identity; antenna-to-leg transformation is accepted and identity is now traced to genes within the appendage, but these specimens were never re-examined.

156.verdict: Light colour tunes tyrosinase to produce colour adaptation; not supported
156.why: Przibram and Brecher claimed blue and yellow light directly slow or speed tyrosinase through changes in acidity, explaining colour adaptation; this found no later confirmation, and colour adaptation runs through sense organs and hormones, though their red intermediate of melanin formation holds.

157.verdict: Photochemical enzyme theory of colouration and its inheritance; not supported
157.why: Przibram’s theory held that light-, heat- and acid-sensitive enzymes directly produce colour adaptation, that induced colours reach the germ cells to form colour races, and that colour vision works photographically; all three ideas were abandoned, leaving only the older tyrosinase–melanin link.

158.verdict: Air exclusion preserves tyrosinase activity; consistent, not re-tested
158.why: Przibram and Dembowski found honey-fungus tyrosinase keeps its activity for months when sealed without air, consistent with its oxygen-dependent chemistry; their claim that yellow light pre-activates the enzyme has no later support, and their colour regressions fit later-described melanin intermediates.

159.verdict: Dark pupae on black backgrounds hold; ultraviolet, eye-independent explanation fails
159.why: Brecher traced darker pupae on black backgrounds to reflected ultraviolet and, because black-lacquered larvae still responded, held the cue independent of vision; the background and wavelength effects fit later work, but black reflects little ultraviolet and her 1924 lacquer experiments showed the cue is seen.
159.open: Whether ultraviolet light itself darkens Pieris brassicae pupae, as her quinine-sulphate filters (lighter pupae on black) and spectrum experiment (darkest pupae in ultraviolet) indicated; no test since her own Part VII (1922) is known.
159.test: Rear wandering P. brassicae larvae on black backgrounds under broad-spectrum light with or without a UV-blocking filter matched for visible transmission, some with stemmata painted over; score pupal melanisation by reflectance spectrometry.

160.verdict: Heritable nuptial pads in water-bred midwife toads; never replicated
160.why: Claimed midwife toads forced to breed in water develop nuptial pads from the grandchild generation, growing over generations; never replicated, the surviving specimen's pad was found ink-injected (Noble 1926), and epigenetic reinterpretations remain speculative.

161.verdict: Iris depigments after lens removal; passive 'iris-sac' explanation superseded
161.why: Uhlenhuth confirmed iris depigmentation after lens removal, with shed pigment taken up by leukocytes, but explained it as passive expulsion when aqueous humour enters a torn 'iris sac', pigment blocking division; modern accounts treat dedifferentiation as an active, signal-driven programme.

162.verdict: One catfish eye with a second lens; description only
162.why: Kolmer describes one catfish eye containing a second, lens-like body and explicitly leaves its origin (iris versus primary lens vesicle) undecided; it is a single-specimen description with no general claim to test.

163.verdict: Carp teeth and calluses cited for Lamarckian inheritance; framework rejected
163.why: Argued that a carp pharyngeal tooth which never chewed still bore a grinding surface, and that pre-formed calluses show use-acquired traits become hereditary; such pre-formed traits are now explained by selection or genetic assimilation, not Lamarckian inheritance.

164.verdict: Hermaphrodite-gland theory of homosexuality not supported; rodent graft results repeated
164.why: Steinach argued that mixed-sex (‘hermaphrodite’) puberty glands cause intersex traits and homosexuality, citing grafted guinea pigs, castration-and-implant operations on homosexual men and a goat with ovotestes; no later work supports a gonadal cause of sexual orientation, though the rodent graft results were repeated.

165.verdict: Distinctive testis histology in homosexual men; not supported
165.why: Steinach described atrophic tubules, fewer Leydig cells and large ‘F-cells’ in testes removed from five homosexual men, compared only with cryptorchid testes, and proposed them as a diagnostic marker; no later work has confirmed any testicular marker of sexual orientation.

166.verdict: Single-case skeletal description of an intersex person; no claim to assess
166.why: A measured description of one intersex person’s skeleton, showing mixed male and female traits, unusually long limbs and many anomalies; its closing link to gonadal secretion restates the view of the time rather than testing a claim.

167.verdict: Size variants after Paramecium 'endomixis'; process reinterpreted as autogamy
167.why: Reported that each 'endomixis' in pure Paramecium aurelia lines yields sublines with new heritable mean sizes; endomixis was later identified as autogamy, a meiotic self-fertilisation, so segregation and new-macronucleus differences, not a failure of the genotype concept, would explain them.

168.verdict: Wound responses as passive physics without 'stimulus'; not the modern view
168.why: This theoretical conclusion to Part I (no new data) argues that wound responses such as iris depigmentation are passive physico-chemical events needing no 'stimulus'; the depigmentation is real, but modern work treats iris dedifferentiation as an active, injury-signal-driven cellular programme.

169.verdict: Heat boosts virility in rats and humans; not supported
169.why: Rats kept warm matured earlier than rats in unheated stalls, which the authors read as heat-boosted, heritable virility explaining racial differences; the rat work was never re-tested, heat is now known to impair the testis, and the inheritance and ‘race’ claims are not supported.

170.verdict: Light acting on blood tyrosinase sets pupal colour; not supported
170.why: Brecher proposed that coloured light shifts the acidity of the caterpillar’s blood tyrosinase, directly setting pupal melanin and green; pupal colour is now understood to be set through neuroendocrine signals and pigment-gene expression, with green from bilin–protein complexes, so this chemism is not supported.

171.verdict: No separate DOPA-oxidase needed; its reaction mechanism and albinism account failed
171.why: Argued that Bloch’s separate ‘Dopa-oxidase’ is unnecessary because tyrosinase blackens DOPA and tyrosine alike, making tyrosine the likely melanin precursor; that fits the modern tyrosinase pathway, but its side-chain mechanism, equal-rate claim and acidity explanation of albinism did not hold.

172.verdict: Pale pupae on white backgrounds hold; infrared-ray explanation superseded
172.why: Attributed pale pupae on white backgrounds to infrared (heat) rays and traced every pupal colour to specific radiation effects; Brecher’s 1924 eye experiments and later neuroendocrine work place the cue in larval vision, so the white-background effect stands but not its infrared explanation.
172.open: Whether warmth or near-infrared light during the pre-pupal sensitive period, independently of the visible background, lightens Pieris brassicae pupae, as her heat and infrared-filter experiments suggested.
172.test: Rear wandering P. brassicae larvae on identical grey backgrounds at 18 versus 30 °C, and at fixed temperature with or without a near-infrared-blocking filter; score pupal melanisation and opacity by reflectance spectrometry.

173.verdict: Rat gestation length unaffected by rearing temperature; consistent with later knowledge
173.why: Found rat litter-to-litter intervals (about 24 days) unchanged across constant 5–40 °C; mammalian gestation is generally buffered against ambient temperature, though his 'secondary homeothermy' explanation assumed body-temperature swings now thought exaggerated.

174.verdict: Triple limbs from breaks: true for injuries, not a universal rule
174.why: Przibram argued that all Bateson-rule triple limbs arise regeneratively at a break with two wound surfaces; injury-induced mirror-image supernumeraries are real, but many triplications are genetic (e.g. Hoge's Mendelian Drosophila reduplications) and positional-confrontation models replaced the break mechanism.
174.open: Whether the mirror-image middle claw of an injury-induced triplication in heterochelous decapods always keeps its own side's claw type, as Przibram inferred from museum specimens, has never been tested experimentally.
174.test: Induce supernumerary chelae in juvenile lobsters or snapping shrimp by partial claw fractures or lateral wounds (as Murayama did in crayfish); score crusher/cutter identity, handedness and symmetry of each component.

175.verdict: One-page review of a growth-speed rule of form; nothing to test
175.why: A one-page review of Karl Przibram's proposal that faster growth yields elongated, branched forms; it reports no data, and the rule, argued from examples such as etiolation, Daphnia helmets and warm-reared mice, never became an accepted principle of organic form.
